analysis.one_liner: Makes Washington, D.C. the 51st state, giving its residents full voting representation in Congress.
analysis.headline: With 133 Democratic cosponsors signed on, the bill was referred to two House committees, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would admit most of the District of Columbia as the State of New Columbia, on equal footing with the other states. D.C. voters would first have to approve statehood in an election; if they did, the state would elect two senators and one voting representative, which every other state's residents already have. A small federal district containing the White House, the Capitol, the Supreme Court, and the main federal office buildings would remain under Congress's control, and federal property would stay exempt from state taxes.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 650,000 people who live in the District of Columbia. They pay federal taxes, serve in the military, and vote in presidential elections, but today have no voting senators or representative in Congress. Under this bill they would elect two senators and one voting House member and their local government would stop being subject to congressional override.
analysis.who_benefits_short: D.C. residents paying federal taxes without a vote

how_it_helps.text: Declares most of the District of Columbia a state 'on an equal footing with the other States in all respects,' following a vote of approval by D.C. voters.
Provides for the first election of two senators and one voting representative from the new state, who would be seated with full rights and privileges.

Transfers the Mayor, Council members, and D.C. executive and judicial officers into the corresponding offices of the new state, so residents would gain full self-government rather than remaining under Congress's authority.
Keeps a small federal district containing the White House, Capitol, Supreme Court, and principal federal monuments as the seat of the national government, so the federal government is not displaced.
Continues all existing D.C. laws, pending court cases, and U.S. citizenship for residents, so admission does not disrupt daily life.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would take on the cost of a new state government for services and functions currently handled with federal involvement, and the new state would be barred from taxing federal land inside its borders. Politically, opponents argued it would add two senators who would reliably vote with one party, shifting the balance of the Senate.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and the party out of power in the Senate

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a new state by ordinary legislation covering a very small territory, and it requires an expedited constitutional amendment to repeal the 23rd Amendment (which currently gives the District presidential electors) — critics argue that this shows statehood raises constitutional questions that a simple statute sidesteps.

The new state would be prohibited from imposing any taxes on federal land within its borders except as Congress permits, so a large share of the city's real estate would remain off its tax rolls while it takes on the full costs of statehood.

The state's voters would only ratify the arrangement in an election, and if even one of the required propositions failed, the entire act would cease to be effective — so the process depends on a single up-or-down local vote on a package of detailed terms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For D.C. residents, the benefit is fundamental: full voting representation in Congress and self-government, which no other group of U.S. citizens is denied. The costs are real but modest — a new state government's expense and the constitutional objection to admitting a small state by statute — and the bill tried to address the sharpest one by carving out a tiny federal enclave and requiring local voter approval. The main obstacle was not the bill's design but the political fact that two new senators would shift the Senate's balance.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Oversight and Government Reform and Rules committees on the day it was introduced, and neither committee ever held a hearing or voted it out before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Eleanor Holmes Norton, the District's non-voting delegate, introduced the New Columbia Admission Act on January 13, 2015.
133 House members, all Democrats, signed on as cosponsors.

The bill was referred to the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform and also to the Committee on Rules; the recorded action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action at any point in the 114th Congress.
The bill expired with the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017, and D.C. residents remained without voting representation.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of D.C. statehood kept the status quo without ever having to vote on it, while the District's roughly 650,000 residents remained the only U.S. citizens taxed by Congress without voting representation in it. House members who never had to take a recorded position were spared a politically charged vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opponents of D.C. statehood kept the status quo

for.name: Eleanor Holmes Norton
for.role: Delegate, District of Columbia (non-voting House member)
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on January 13, 2015.

for.name: 133 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill a large Democratic majority of the House behind it from day one.

against.name: Jason Chaffetz
against.role: Chair, House Oversight and Government Reform Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee of primary referral took no recorded action on the bill — no hearing, no markup — for the full two-year Congress.

against.name: Paul Ryan
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor consideration; it never left committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 133 cosponsors were Democrats and none were Republicans; the bill then sat in the committees of the Republican-controlled House until the Congress ended.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and the two major parties
industries.note: Admitting the new state would seat two senators and one voting representative, shifting the Senate's balance of power — the concentrated political stake in the bill. Democrats sponsoring it and residents seeking representation pull in the same direction; opponents' interest in preserving the existing Senate balance runs against D.C. residents' vote.

The bill keeps federal title to federal property and reserves exclusive federal authority over military lands, and bars the new state from taxing federal property — so the federal government loses no land or revenue while residents gain a state.
